note: Curated waypoint descriptions, keyed by the stable ids in data/waypoint-ids.json. Applied by scripts/build-trails.ts (overriding any description from the GPX/GeoJSON source) and uploadable to the comments API with scripts/upload-descriptions.ts. Listed north to south, matching the km order of the generated trail data, with off-route waypoints appended at the end. Campsite facilities are described in the general terms that hold across the track's shelters; the state of any individual rainwater tank is not something this text can promise.

descriptions.name: Kalamunda MTB park
descriptions.description: Mountain bike park in the Perth Hills with a cafe and toilets, and the first easy stop out of Kalamunda. A good place for a coffee before the walking settles into jarrah forest.

descriptions.name: Hewitt's Hill Campsite
descriptions.description: The first Bibbulmun shelter south of Kalamunda, close enough to walk to in an afternoon. Standard setup: three-sided timber shelter with a sleeping platform, tent sites, pit toilet, picnic table and a rainwater tank. Treat tank water before you drink it.

descriptions.name: Mundaring Weir hotel
descriptions.description: Pub near Mundaring Weir, a long-standing stop for a meal and a cold drink early in the walk. Worth confirming it is open before you build a night around it.

descriptions.name: Ball Creek Campsite
descriptions.description: Timber shelter camp in the jarrah forest above Ball Creek, with a sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank. The creek is seasonal, so don't expect running water outside winter and spring.

descriptions.name: Helena Campsite
descriptions.description: Campsite on the slopes above the Helena valley, with the usual shelter, sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and tank. Tank water needs treating, and levels can be low by the end of summer.

descriptions.name: Waalegh Campsite
descriptions.description: Ridge-top shelter with long views out over the Darling Scarp, one of the better outlooks in the northern section. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank; there is no natural water up here.

descriptions.name: Beraking Campsite
descriptions.description: Jarrah and wandoo forest camp with the standard three-sided shelter, sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and tank. Fill up here if the next stage is a long one, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Mt Dale
descriptions.description: Camp marked near Mount Dale, a granite-topped hill in the Perth Hills forest. Facilities here are basic and may not include a tank, so carry the water you need rather than planning to collect it.

descriptions.name: Brookton Campsite
descriptions.description: Forest shelter camp close to the Brookton Highway crossing, with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank. A common first or last night for people walking just the northern section.

descriptions.name: Brookton Highway
descriptions.description: Sealed road crossing where the track meets Brookton Highway. Traffic runs steadily between Perth and the Wheatbelt, so cross with care; the road is also a practical spot for a lift or a food drop.

descriptions.name: Canning Campsite
descriptions.description: Shelter camp near the Canning River, with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank. The river can run in winter and spring but is not dependable, and anything you collect should be treated.

descriptions.name: Monadnocks Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp among the Monadnocks, the granite domes that give this stretch its steep climbs. Usual shelter, tent sites, toilet and tank; the ups and downs either side make it worth arriving with water in hand.

descriptions.name: Mt Cooke Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp below Mount Cooke, the high point of the Darling Range and the biggest climb in the northern half. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and a tank, which is the only water — check the level as soon as you arrive.

descriptions.name: Nerang Campsite
descriptions.description: Quiet jarrah-forest shelter with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and tank. It sits in a long run of forest between towns, so plan food and water around the town gaps rather than the camps.

descriptions.name: Ginger Creek
descriptions.description: Camp marked at Ginger Creek in the forest shortly before the Albany Highway crossing. Facilities are basic and the creek is seasonal, so treat it as a fallback rather than a planned water stop.

descriptions.name: Albany Highway
descriptions.description: Where the track meets Albany Highway, marked here as a camp. The highway is a fast sealed road between Perth and the south coast — cross carefully — and it is a practical place to arrange a lift or a drop.

descriptions.name: White Horse
descriptions.description: Camp marked in the White Horse Hills country between Albany Highway and Mount Wells. Expect a basic bush site rather than a full Bibbulmun shelter, and carry your water in.

descriptions.name: Mt Wells
descriptions.description: One of the few Bibbulmun camps with an enclosed hut rather than an open shelter — a former forestry building on Mount Wells, with an old fire lookout nearby. Tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank that needs treating.

descriptions.name: Chadora
descriptions.description: Forest shelter camp in the jarrah south of Mount Wells, with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank. The last camp before the walk down into Dwellingup.

descriptions.name: Dwelingup
descriptions.description: Small jarrah timber town sitting right on the track, and the first proper resupply south of Perth, with shops, food, beds and a campground. A common spot for a rest day or a posted resupply box.

descriptions.name: Swamp Oak Campsite
descriptions.description: Shelter camp in the forest south of Dwellingup, with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and tank. An easy first night out of town on a mostly gentle stage.

descriptions.name: Murray Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp above the Murray River, one of the more scenic spots in this section, with shelter, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank. River water below is worth treating if you use it.

descriptions.name: Dookanelly Campsite
descriptions.description: Standard Bibbulmun shelter in the forest, with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank. Long stages either side make it a sensible place to fill up, tank permitting.

descriptions.name: Possum Springs Campsite
descriptions.description: Forest campsite named for springs nearby, with the usual shelter, tent sites, toilet and tank. Springs in this country are seasonal, so plan around the tank and treat whatever you collect.

descriptions.name: Yourdamung Campsite
descriptions.description: Shelter camp near Yourdamung Lake in the forest north of Collie, with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and tank. The lake is shallow and seasonal and is not a water source to plan on.

descriptions.name: Harris Dam campsite
descriptions.description: Camp near Harris Dam, the reservoir that supplies Collie. It is a drinking-water catchment with access restrictions, so plan on the campsite tank rather than the water you can see.

descriptions.name: Collie
descriptions.description: Coal and power town, and the largest centre anywhere near the middle of the track, with supermarkets, pubs, accommodation and transport connections. The standard mid-track resupply and rest stop.

descriptions.name: Yabberup Campsite
descriptions.description: Quiet forest shelter with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank, and the first camp out of Collie. Treat tank water, and check the level before committing to a dry stage.

descriptions.name: Mumbullup Pub
descriptions.description: Small country tavern near the track between Collie and Balingup, a long-standing walkers' stop for a meal and a cold drink. It is a tiny settlement, so check the hours before you count on it.

descriptions.name: Noggenup Campsite
descriptions.description: Shelter camp in the forest with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank. The tank is the only water here and can run low, so arrive with something in reserve.

descriptions.name: Grimwade Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp in the forest near the old timber settlement of Grimwade, with the usual shelter, tent sites, toilet and tank. The last night before the descent into the Balingup valley.

descriptions.name: Balingup
descriptions.description: Small hills town in a green farming valley, known for its gardens and craft shops, with a store, food and accommodation. A pleasant short-stop resupply, smaller than Collie.

descriptions.name: Blackwood camp
descriptions.description: Shelter camp above the Blackwood River, with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank. The river is a genuine watercourse but still needs treating, and the valley sides are steep either way out.

descriptions.name: Gregory Brook campsite
descriptions.description: Campsite by Gregory Brook in mixed jarrah and karri country, with shelter, tent sites, toilet and tank. The brook is seasonal; treat any water you take, from the brook or the tank.

descriptions.name: Broackman Highway
descriptions.description: Where the track meets Brockman Highway, marked here as a camp. It is a sealed road and a practical access point for a lift or a drop, but not a serviced campsite.

descriptions.name: Willow springs
descriptions.description: Willow Springs shelter camp in the forest, with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank. The spring that gives it the name is not something to rely on.

descriptions.name: Donnelly River Village
descriptions.description: Former timber mill town, now a small holiday village on the track with a general store and cottage accommodation, and tame kangaroos and emus wandering the streets. It is a village top-up, not a full resupply.

descriptions.name: Tom road campsite
descriptions.description: Forest shelter camp off Tom Road, with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank. A straightforward overnight stop in tall timber; treat the tank water.

descriptions.name: Greens Island? (non-bibb)
descriptions.description: Marked as a camping option off the official Bibbulmun route, and the question mark in the name means the source itself was unsure. Expect no facilities and carry your own water.

descriptions.name: Boarding House campsite
descriptions.description: Shelter camp deep in the karri country, with sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank. There is no dependable water beyond the tank, so treat it and check what is in it.

descriptions.name: Beavis Campsite
descriptions.description: Standard Bibbulmun camp in the forest between Donnelly River and Pemberton, with shelter, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank. Treat the tank water; there is nothing else here.

descriptions.name: Beedelup Campsite
descriptions.description: Campsite in Beedelup National Park, karri forest country not far from Beedelup Falls. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank; the falls run hard after winter rain and thin out by late summer.

descriptions.name: Pemberton
descriptions.description: Karri forest town and one of the best resupply points on the southern half, with a supermarket, cafes, pubs and a range of accommodation. A common rest-day stop before the forest run to Northcliffe.

descriptions.name: Gloucester Tree
descriptions.description: Giant karri fitted with a spiral of steel pegs as a fire lookout tree, and one of the few still open to climb. There is a picnic area at the base, a few kilometres along the track out of Pemberton.

descriptions.name: Warren Campsite
descriptions.description: Shelter camp in the Warren River valley, among some of the tallest karri on the whole track. Sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and a tank; the river is close by but should be treated if you use it.

descriptions.name: Schafer Campsite
descriptions.description: Forest campsite with the usual three-sided shelter, sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank. The last camp before the walk into Northcliffe.

descriptions.name: Northcliffe
descriptions.description: Small timber and farming town on the track, with a store, a pub and modest accommodation. Enough for a resupply but not a large one, and it is the last town before the long remote stretch to Walpole.

descriptions.name: Gardner Campsite
descriptions.description: First camp south of Northcliffe, in the low forest and swamp country that opens this remote section. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank, with no dependable natural water nearby.

descriptions.name: Lake Maringup Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp beside Lake Maringup, a large shallow tannin-stained lake in remote wetland country. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and a tank; lake water is dark and needs treating, and the lake shrinks a long way in a dry year.

descriptions.name: Dog Pool campsite
descriptions.description: Campsite by a pool on the Shannon River, one of the few places in this section with real running water. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and tank; river water here is tannin-stained and should be treated.

descriptions.name: Mt Chance Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp below Mount Chance, a granite rise in an otherwise flat run of heath and swamp — the short climb up is worth it for the view. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank.

descriptions.name: Woolbales
descriptions.description: Camp near the Woolbales Hills in remote heathland, big skies and very little shade. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and a tank that is the only water — check it early and plan the next stage around what you find.

descriptions.name: Long Point
descriptions.description: Campsite on a rise looking out over Broke Inlet, one of the standout outlooks on the southern half. The usual shelter, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank; the inlet is brackish, so the tank is the water.

descriptions.name: Mount Clare
descriptions.description: Shelter camp near Mount Clare, the last night out for most walkers before Walpole. Sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and a tank — treat the water and check the level on arrival.

descriptions.name: Walpole
descriptions.description: Small town on the Walpole and Nornalup inlets, with a store, pub, cafes and accommodation, and the resupply that ends the long remote stretch from Northcliffe. The track turns coastal from here.

descriptions.name: Franklin River Campsite
descriptions.description: Campsite near the Frankland River in tall tingle and karri forest. Shelter, sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank; the river runs nearby but is tannin-stained and worth treating.

descriptions.name: Tree Top Walk
descriptions.description: The Valley of the Giants Tree Top Walk: a steel walkway carried up through the crowns of huge red tingle trees, with a ground-level boardwalk among the buttressed trunks below. A paid attraction with a visitor centre, and some of the biggest trees on the track.

descriptions.name: Giants Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp in the tingle forest close to the Valley of the Giants, an easy stop if you have spent part of the day at the Tree Top Walk. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank.

descriptions.name: Sout Coast highway
descriptions.description: Crossing of the South Coast Highway, the main sealed road along this coast. Traffic moves fast here, so cross carefully; it is also the obvious place to arrange a lift into Walpole or Denmark.

descriptions.name: Rame Head Campsite
descriptions.description: Coastal campsite on the headland at Rame Head, with a wide view over the Southern Ocean. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank; the site is exposed, so pitch with the wind in mind.

descriptions.name: Peaceful Bay
descriptions.description: Small holiday settlement on the coast with a caravan park and a general store — enough for a top-up and a meal rather than a full resupply. Things can be quiet outside the holiday seasons.

descriptions.name: Canoe crossing
descriptions.description: One of the Bibbulmun's set pieces: canoes are left on the inlet banks for walkers, with the convention that you leave one on each side for whoever comes next. Check the wind and water before you push off, and don't cross in rough conditions.

descriptions.name: Boat harbour campsite
descriptions.description: Coastal camp near Boat Harbour, tucked into the scrub behind the beach. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank; there is no fresh water along this coast, so the tank is it — check and treat.

descriptions.name: Parry Beach (paid)
descriptions.description: Vehicle-accessible beachside campground rather than a Bibbulmun shelter, so a fee applies and it can fill up in holiday periods. Being a road camp it usually has better facilities than the track sites.

descriptions.name: Parry Inlet
descriptions.description: Inlet crossing just along from Parry Beach. It is usually a shallow wade or a walk across the sandbar, but it can be deep and flowing after rain or once the bar opens — look at it before you commit.

descriptions.name: William bay campsite
descriptions.description: Campsite in William Bay National Park, the granite and white-sand country that takes in Greens Pool and Elephant Rocks. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank.

descriptions.name: Denmark
descriptions.description: Riverside town on Wilson Inlet with supermarkets, cafes, pubs and plenty of accommodation — the best resupply between Walpole and Albany, and an easy place to lose a rest day.

descriptions.name: Wilson Inlet (risky crossing if flowing)
descriptions.description: Crossing of the Wilson Inlet sandbar. With the bar closed it is a straightforward walk on sand; once it has been opened or is flowing, the channel is fast and deep and the safe answer is to turn back and go around.

descriptions.name: Nullaki Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp on the Nullaki Peninsula, in coastal heath between the inlet and the ocean. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank, and no natural water at all — arrive with a reserve.

descriptions.name: West Cape Howe Campsite
descriptions.description: Campsite in West Cape Howe National Park, near the southernmost point of Western Australia, with cliffs and exposed heath. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and a rainwater tank; the wind here can be relentless.

descriptions.name: Shelly Beach (non-bibb)
descriptions.description: Road-accessible campground near Shelly Beach rather than an official Bibbulmun site. Fees and booking rules may apply, and the facilities are those of a national park camp, not a track shelter.

descriptions.name: Torbay Campsite
descriptions.description: Bibbulmun shelter camp near Torbay, back in the coastal scrub. Sleeping platform, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank; treat what you take, and don't assume a full tank late in a dry summer.

descriptions.name: Cosy Corner (non-bibb)
descriptions.description: Coastal camping and day-use area off the official route rather than a Bibbulmun site. It is vehicle-accessible and popular with campers and fishers, so expect company over summer.

descriptions.name: Torbay Inlet
descriptions.description: Inlet crossing near Torbay. Usually a shallow wade or a sandbar walk, but depth and flow change with rain and with whether the bar is open, so have a look before you step in.

descriptions.name: Muttonbird Campsite
descriptions.description: Coastal shelter camp near Muttonbird Beach, open to the Southern Ocean. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and a tank that is the only water here, so treat it and check what is left in it.

descriptions.name: Sandpatch Campsite
descriptions.description: The last camp before Albany, up on the Sandpatch where the wind farm turbines line the cliffs. Shelter, tent sites, toilet and rainwater tank — and very little cover from the wind that runs the turbines.

descriptions.name: Albany
descriptions.description: The southern end of the Bibbulmun Track, on King George Sound. The walk finishes at the terminus marker on the Albany waterfront, and the town has full services and transport back to Perth.

descriptions.name: Can hitch from here
descriptions.description: Marked on the hitch-into-Denmark variation as a spot to try for a lift rather than walk the road in. A lift is never something to count on, so treat this as a bail-out option and not part of the plan.
